key_concepts.summary: Stance controls balance, punch availability, defensive readiness, and movement options.
Guard is not a static shell; it changes with range, punch, angle, fatigue, and opponent threat.
A boxer must enter, exit, pivot, and reset before complex combinations are useful.
Effective punching uses foot pressure, hip/trunk rotation, shoulder/scapular control, and timing.
Good defense creates a counter, exit, clinch, or reset instead of just avoiding punches.
Conditioning must not repeatedly reinforce poor mechanics.

tactical_rules.rule: Teach jab as range, rhythm, defense disruption, and setup before treating it only as a scoring punch.
Do not progress rear-hand power before the athlete can rotate without falling forward.
Hooks should be taught with elbow/wrist structure and hip rotation; beginners should not swing wide under fatigue.
Every defensive drill should include a reset, counter, angle, or clinch decision.
Increase combination length only when stance and guard return remain stable.
New technique can be introduced through shadow, bag, pads, partner touch, then controlled sparring.

physical_demands.quality: hips, calves, feet, and trunk maintain shape under repeated movement.
hips and trunk transfer force into punching.
shoulder blade control supports speed, guard return, and impact tolerance.
head position and trunk stiffness support defense and balance.
repeat fast punches while preserving guard and accuracy.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Heavy bag/pad volume with poor wrapping or alignment can irritate hand and wrist.
High shoulder fatigue can degrade guard and punching mechanics.
Neck fatigue can reduce head-position control during contact.
Repeated rotation without hip mobility/trunk control may irritate the back.
Poor pivot mechanics can overload knee/ankle during hooks and angle changes.

training_implications.summary: Use shadowboxing to teach posture, rhythm, and coordination before impact.
Bag rounds should target rhythm, power, accuracy, defense returns, or conditioning, not random exhaustion.
Pad work should teach timing, range, defensive return, and tactical cues.
Defense should progress from rehearsed to variable before harder contact.
Warmups should include wrist, shoulder, scapular, trunk, and neck prep for boxing sessions.
